papers.title: Molecularly Engineered Nitrate Double Perovskites with Elevated Ferroelectric Phase Transition Temperature and Large Piezoelectric Response
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Conventional ABX 3 perovskites place organic species at A ‐sites or as X ‐site linkers, where the B ‐site is reserved for metals. Molecular double perovskites with a general formula A 2 B I B III X 6 possess higher tunability and distinct B I ‐sites that can accommodate small cations, further regulating lattice connectivity and physical properties. Here, we introduce a new family of B I ‐site‐organic nitrate double perovskites, (RM3HQ) 2 B I Eu(NO 3 ) 6 (RM3HQ = ( R )‐ N ‐methyl‐3‐hydroxyquinuclidinium), forming compounds 1 – 4 with B I = ammonium, methylammonium, formamidinium, and dimethylammonium, respectively. Compounds 1 and 2 adopt mixed corner‐/face‐sharing non‐perovskite structures, whereas 3 and 4 form double perovskites. This structural variation raises the ferroelectric phase‐transition temperature to 349 K in 4 and 414 K in 3 , much higher than that of the inorganic analogue ( T c = 285 K). This further widens the temperature margin for stable room‐temperature piezoelectric responses, as demonstrated in 3 by ferroelectric hysteresis loops, ferroelastic domains, and a large piezoelectric coefficient (| d 33 | ≈ 56 pC N −1 ). During these phase transitions, the Eu 3+ photoluminescence intensity ratio (616 nm/ 592 nm) increases from 0.32 to 2.92 in 3 and from 0.37 to 4.59 in 4 , reflecting transition‐related changes in the ligand field. This work highlights the B I ‐site as an effective handle for tuning ferroelectric phase‐transition temperatures and tunable Eu 3+ photoluminescence.

papers.title: Kinetic Limitations of Single-Atom Catalysts in Hydrazine Oxidation
papers.abstract: Abstract Single-atom catalysts (SACs) have attracted considerable interest, displaying impressive performance for a wide plethora of electrocatalytic reactions. However, the important question whether isolated sites are always beneficial remains unresolved. Here, by using the hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR) as a model reaction, we examine how isolated single-atom metal sites restrict the adsorption mode of intermediates to the monodentate configuration, which leads to weak intermediate stabilization and poor reaction kinetics. This contrasts with bulk metal sites where availability of the bidentate adsorption configuration offers better intermediate stabilization and dehydrogenation kinetics. As a result, Ir, Pt, and Pd SACs were found to require high HzOR overpotentials of 0.90, 1.21, and 1.19 V at 3 mA cm–2, respectively. Comparatively, their Ir, Pt, Pd nanoparticle counterparts with similar metal loading exhibit considerably lower overpotentials of only 0.35, 0.83, and 0.64 V at 3 mA cm–2, respectively. Taken together, our work contributes towards a more complete understanding of SACs, emphasizing the importance of considering site structure and the mechanistic demands of the reaction.

Anti‐Poisoning Tin Single‐Atom Unlocks High‐Activity Ruthenium Catalysts for Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
Engineering Thermoelectric‐Electrocatalytic Coupling in RuO2/PrCoO3 Heterointerface for Efficient Oxygen Evolution
Stabilizing Ru Sites via Lattice Oxygen Locking of Nb‐Ru/RuO 2 to Break the Activity–Stability Trade‐Off for Acidic Oxygen Evolution
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Developing highly active and stable Ru‐based catalysts for the acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is essential to accelerate the industrialization of proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE). However, Ru‐based catalysts inevitably follow the lattice oxygen mechanism (LOM) during the actual reaction, which in turn triggers severe Ru dissolution. While shifting the reaction pathway to the adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM) improves stability, it often compromises catalytic activity. Herein, we design an Nb‐doped Ru/RuO 2 heterostructure catalyst to inhibit the unstable LOM, and concurrently propose a favorable Brønsted Site‐Promoted Proton Transfer (BSPT) mechanism derived from the AEM. Specifically, the synergy between Nb doping and Ru/RuO 2 heterostructure enhances activity by improving deprotonation capability and optimizing oxygen‐intermediate adsorption, while simultaneously improving durability by stabilizing lattice oxygen and suppressing excessive oxidation and dissolution of Ru. Consequently, the Nb‐Ru/RuO 2 delivers an overpotential of 186 mV at 10 mA cm −2 with impressive durability over 3000 h. In a working PEMWE, it exhibits remarkable durability for 3000, 1200, and 900 h at 500, 1000, and 2000 mA cm −2 . This study offers novel design principles and theoretical foundations to advance efficient, low‐cost PEMWE hydrogen production.

papers.title: The Potential of Zero Charge: An Interfacial Descriptor Governing Hydrogen Evolution Reaction on Bulk Metal Electrodes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT While the Sabatier‐based volcano plots guide catalyst design for Hydrogen Evolution Reaction (HER), the purely thermodynamic hydrogen binding energy descriptor fails to capture experimental HER trends accurately due to the omission of kinetic contributions. Herein, we combine the fixed‐potential method with our developed continuous proton supply/consumption model to establish an extra kinetic descriptor for metal‐based electrodes (Pt, Pd, Au, Ag, and their bimetallic alloys) under practical working conditions. The potential of zero charge (PZC) is demonstrated to be the interfacial descriptor, which modulates surface charge density and thereby tunes the kinetic proton enrichment within the EDL. Building on this insight, the PZC is integrated with hydrogen binding energies to establish a new two‐dimensional volcano plot for HER. The updated volcano plot derived from the dual descriptors effectively matches the experimental results, which provides an additional guiding parameter for rational catalyst design.

papers.title: Synergistic Charge Scavenging in Pt/C‐Polyoxometalate Systems for Scalable Biomass Power Generation via Super‐Reduced Electrolytes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Direct electrochemical conversion of unrefined biomass waste into electricity offers a sustainable pathway for decentralized energy generation, yet its practical implementation has been fundamentally hindered by low power densities and limited scalability. A fundamental bottleneck lies in the intrinsic recalcitrance of biomass, which restricts electron harvesting to shallow oxidation pathways and confines redox mediators to low reduction states. Here, we demonstrate a scalable biomass flow fuel cell (BFFC) enabled by a super‐reduced polyoxometalate (POM) electrolyte that overcomes the long‐standing electron‐harvesting ceiling. By employing a catalytic oxidative degradation strategy that promotes extensive cleavage of recalcitrant C─C linkages in the lignocellulosic matrix, we unlock deep multi‐electron reduction of POM, achieving an electron transfer capacity exceeding four electrons per molecule. As a result, the single‐cell device delivers a record‐breaking power density of 218.6 mW cm − 2 . Beyond laboratory‐scale demonstrations, we constructed a 10‐cell stack prototype, producing 59.2 Wh over 15.6 h of stable operation directly from raw biomass.

papers.title: Aligned Self-Assembled Nanostructure by Chemical Force Trigger, Biased Migration, and Oscillatory Hydrogel Growth
papers.abstract: Abstract Cells generate pico-to-nanonewton forces through metabolic circuits and diffusion for downstream processes, including stress fiber assembly and cellular growth. The inherent complexities of the system’s processing, reactivity, and adaptability make it difficult to recapitulate in a synthetic setting. Herein, we compartmentalized the urease-urea feedback-controlled reaction network (FCRN), demonstrating global vs local function adaptability by coupling with peptide self-assembly. Compartmentalized FCRN (c-FCRN) facilitates chemical energy-to-mechanical energy conversion, creating forces on the piconewton scale, allowing nanofiber alignment, akin to what a cell does. The trade-off between multiple microscale interactions in the chemo-material network implies molecular-biased migration resembling chemotactic-like directed motion in synthetic settings, which promotes spatial self-assembly remodelling. Consequently, regulating the reaction-diffusion chemistry, we demonstrate oscillatory hydrogel growth by encasing the c-FCRN with a physical membrane barrier. Furthermore, c-FCRN provides a rudimentary structure-building system to create various complex hydrogel structures, bypassing the 3D printing tools. Thus, the chemo-material network provides proof-of-concept for biomimetic material development by emulating biologically inspired technologies.
